title: Predestination: Calvinism, Free Will, and Islamic Qadar Compared
summary: Comparing Calvinist predestination, Arminian free will, and Islamic Qadar — three serious theological positions on the same underlying question.

body.text: A question every serious theological tradition has wrestled with

How do human free will and God's total sovereignty and foreknowledge fit together? This question has produced serious, carefully reasoned positions within both Christianity and Islam — worth comparing directly, since it's a genuinely difficult question in both traditions, not a place where one faith has an easy answer the other lacks.

Calvinist and Reformed Protestant theology holds a strong doctrine of predestination — God has, from eternity, chosen (elected) who will be saved, and human choice, while real in an everyday sense, doesn't ultimately determine salvation outcomes God has already sovereignly decreed. This is a serious, carefully argued theological position within a significant Protestant tradition, not a fringe view.
The Arminian and Catholic/Orthodox position: genuine libertarian free will

Arminian Protestant theology, along with mainstream Catholic and Orthodox teaching, holds that humans possess genuine free will to accept or reject God's grace, with God's foreknowledge of a choice not being the same as God causing that choice — closer, structurally, to the mainstream Sunni Islamic position covered next.
The Islamic position: Qadar and free will held together

As covered in Stage 1's lesson on the Six Articles of Faith, mainstream Sunni theology holds that Allah's complete knowledge and decree over all things (Qadar) coexists with genuine human free will and responsibility — a position generally closer to the Arminian/Catholic model than to strict Calvinist predestination, though Islamic theology has its own internal historical debate on this question too (the classical Jabriyyah, who leaned toward stronger determinism, versus the Qadariyyah and later Ash'ari/Maturidi schools, who worked out different ways of holding divine decree and human responsibility together).

body.translation: Indeed, Allah does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves.

body.text: A genuinely difficult question, not a resolved one, in either faith

It's worth being honest here: exactly how divine foreknowledge and decree relate to genuine human freedom remains, in classical Islamic scholarship's own words, something ultimately beyond full human comprehension, in much the same way Calvinist and Arminian Christians continue to debate this question without full resolution across centuries. This is one of the more genuinely humbling theological questions covered in this whole collection — worth holding with some intellectual humility on both sides.

body.question: Is mainstream Islam closer to Calvinism or to Arminian/Catholic free will theology?
body.answer: Mainstream Sunni Islamic theology (Ash'ari and Maturidi schools especially) is generally closer to the Arminian/Catholic emphasis on genuine, real human responsibility and choice, while still affirming God's complete knowledge and ultimate decree — though, as noted, some historical and minority Islamic positions leaned more deterministic, similar to Calvinism.

body.question: Does believing in Qadar mean a Muslim shouldn't try to change their circumstances?
body.answer: No — mainstream Islamic teaching consistently emphasises genuine effort and real responsibility for one's choices, precisely alongside belief in Qadar; using Qadar as an excuse for inaction or fatalism is explicitly discouraged in mainstream Islamic teaching, not supported by it.

body.question: If you grew up in a Calvinist or strongly predestinarian tradition, does Islam's position on Qadar and free will feel like a meaningful shift, or does it feel familiar?
